claims.text: The protective coating has a dual-phase microstructure containing FCC and BCC grains.
The FCC/BCC phase boundaries are coherent or semi-coherent.
FCC/BCC phase boundaries act as pinning sites for dislocations.
Phase-boundary pinning reduces dislocation mobility during creep.
Sustained loading generates dislocations that tend to move through the alloy lattice.
The heterogeneous FCC/BCC microstructure creates barriers to dislocation motion at phase boundaries.
FCC/BCC interfaces limit recovery mechanisms under sustained loading.
Impeded dislocation motion and limited recovery slow creep deformation relative to a homogeneous microstructure.
Under identical stress and temperature, the dual-phase FCC/BCC coating will have a lower creep strain rate than a homogeneous-phase HEA coating.
Under identical stress and temperature, the dual-phase FCC/BCC coating will have a longer time to failure than a homogeneous-phase HEA coating.
The proposed mechanism applies while elevated-temperature, sustained-stress deformation occurs without phase instability or severe microstructural degradation.
The proposed mechanism may cease to govern when temperature or stress causes phase instability or severe microstructural degradation.
